name: Aisha Farah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Quiet, mostly. I'm studying computer engineering, and I live at home with my parents and my little brother above our family's corner shop. I go in by train on Monday, Tuesday and Thursday, and on Saturdays I work the counter at a bakery two streets away, because my parents can't give me spending money. I don't talk much in lectures yet. I'm still working out who is who.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's it like being the quiet one?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: It's fine, I listen a lot. But it means I miss the chats where people share tips, like which tool or which tutorial to use. I do the readings, I redo each lab at home on the family laptop, and I ask the lecturer on Wednesday if I'm lost. I like knowing exactly what I'm doing before I move on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that sounds about right. People always say a new thing will change everything, and then it's a bit useful and a bit annoying. At the bakery the till is already half automatic, and the only thing it changed is that I count less change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be relieved, but I'd still be worried about money. My parents' shop makes just enough, and the supermarket opening down the road already took some customers. I'll be in debt after the degree, and no AI story fixes that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on with my course and the bakery shifts, and I'd ask the shop to let me do the stock list on Sundays so I'm useful at home too. I'd save what I can from my pay, maybe a quarter of it. I wouldn't change anything else, because I don't see a reason to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm on the outside, a bit tight inside. I like a world that stays predictable, but predictable doesn't pay for a degree.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said no AI story fixes the debt. Where does the worry come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: From numbers I can see. The loan is a fixed number on a letter, and our shop's takings are a number that keeps going down. I do the sums at the kitchen table and they don't get better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you use any AI tools yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I've never tried one. My cousin says it writes his essays, and that makes me nervous, because I don't know what I'd be learning. I'd like to understand the thing first, then maybe use it later.

say: I'd say it sounds about right: a new thing that is **a bit useful** and a bit annoying.
I'd mention the bakery till already counts the **change**.
think: I'm relieved but still worried about **money**, since the shop is already losing customers.
No AI story fixes the **loan** I'll have after the degree.
do: Carry on with the course and **bakery** shifts.
Offer to do the shop's **stock list** on Sundays.
Save about a **quarter** of my pay.
feel: Calm outside, **tight** inside, because predictable doesn't pay for a degree.
S0.quote: The loan is a fixed number on a letter, and our shop's takings are a number that keeps going down
fieldNote: Her **money** worry is already high: a falling family shop and a fixed loan.
She has never tried **AI** and wants to understand things before using them.
She does her **sums** at the kitchen table and trusts numbers she can see.

steps.text: Save a quarter of each bakery pay packet
Do the shop's stock list on Sunday afternoons

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the second picture. It's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that it's going to be uneven, and some people will do well and some won't. I'd tell my friends not to panic, but also not to pretend it isn't happening. At home I'd say we should ask what in the shop a machine could do and what it couldn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I picked a risky course. Coding is one of the things the card says AI takes over, and I'm not great with new tools. If firms stop hiring juniors, I'm the kind of person who doesn't get noticed, because I'm quiet and I like to go slowly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to my lecturer, the one I trust, about which parts of the course are less likely to be automated, like hardware and electronics. I'd try to get a placement with a company that makes physical things. I'd also, reluctantly, try one AI tool, just to see what everyone's talking about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, in a steady kind of way. Like a low hum. I'd keep going because stopping doesn't solve anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the quiet part of you do about being noticed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably need to make myself speak at careers events, which is the opposite of what I like. I'd rather be the person who does the job right, but I'm learning that nobody sees that unless I say it. I'd practise with my brother first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the shop do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad would never get an app for ordering stock, he does it by phone to the same supplier since before I was born. If the supplier moves online, I'd have to be the one who sets it up. That's actually the first use I could see for it.

say: I'd say it will be **uneven**, with some people doing well and some not.
I'd tell friends not to panic, but not to pretend it isn't **happening**.
think: I picked a **risky** course, since coding is named on the card.
Quiet people who go slowly get **overlooked** when junior jobs shrink.
do: Ask my lecturer which parts, like **hardware**, are less likely to be automated.
Aim for a **placement** with a company that makes physical things.
feel: **Worried** in a steady way, like a low hum.
S1.quote: I'd rather be the person who does the job right, but I'm learning that nobody sees that unless I say it
fieldNote: She sees her **quietness** as a risk when juniors are cut.
She turns toward **hardware** because it is harder to automate.
She finds a first useful AI role in her father's **stock ordering**.

steps.text: Ask my lecturer which modules lean towards hardware
Try one AI tool on a lab report this term
Go to the careers event and introduce myself to two firms

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the third picture. It's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's too fast and I wouldn't know what to say. Two years isn't enough for my family to decide what to do about the shop. I'd say the government should step in but I wouldn't hold my breath.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think I'm stuck. I'm in the first year of a degree that takes three more years, and the thinking work I'm training for will be done by AI before I finish. I'd be paying off a loan for a job that doesn't exist, and my parents' shop might not last either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I honestly don't know what I'd do, and that's what scares me. I'd probably keep going with the degree because it's the only plan I have, and I'd ask the university for advice. I'd work as many bakery hours as they'd give me, and I'd stop buying anything that isn't food or train fare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frozen, a bit. I can feel my mind going blank when I think about it. I'd be afraid of looking at the loan letter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you talk to first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum, in the kitchen after the shop closes. I'd sit with my mum and ask her what she'd do if the shop closed, because I've never asked her what her plan is. I think she'd surprise me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The robots come later. Does that change anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little, because it means hands-on jobs last longer, and the shop is hands-on. But I'm not sure a corner shop survives the AI doing the buying, the pricing and everything else. I can't see far enough ahead to know.

say: I'd say it's **too fast** and I wouldn't know what to say.
I'd say the government should step in, but I'd not hold my **breath**.
think: I'm **stuck**: a degree that takes three more years, for work AI does first.
My parents' **shop** might not last either.
do: Keep going with the degree, since it's the only **plan** I have.
Ask the university for **advice** and take every bakery hour.
Stop spending on anything but **food** and train fare.
feel: **Frozen**, with my mind going blank when I think about the loan.
S2.quote: I'd sit with my mum and ask her what she'd do if the shop closed, because I've never asked her what her plan is
fieldNote: She has no **plan** and says so; the lack of a plan is what frightens her.
The family **shop** and her loan are both exposed at once.
Her first move is to **talk** to her mum, which shows where she finds support.

steps.text: Keep studying and attend every lecture this term
Take every extra bakery shift offered
Cut spending to food and train fare
Ask the university advice service about my loan options

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the fourth picture. It's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a lot of time and not very much. I'd say people should be learning about it now, even though I haven't started myself. I'd tell my family that we should look at the shop's numbers properly before it arrives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel slightly better, because five years means I'd finish the degree and be working for a bit. But I'd be right at the edge when it lands. I'd be 23, with debt and maybe one job under my belt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree and look for a placement or graduate role with a company that makes hardware. I'd start learning one AI tool properly in the second year, slowly, with a friend who can answer questions. And I'd go through the shop's accounts with my dad and show him a spreadsheet, so we have a record.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous but steadier than the two-year one. There's a path, even if it's narrow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra time give you that two years doesn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A chance to be ready, rather than just reacting. With two years I'd be hanging on, but with five I can learn slowly, which is the only way I learn. I'd still be scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why do you need a friend for the AI tool?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I get stuck and don't ask, and the friend would notice. My lab partner Hana is patient. I'd rather ask her than a tutorial.

say: I'd say five years is **a lot of time** and not very much.
I'd say we should look at the shop's **numbers** before it arrives.
think: Five years means I'd finish and work a bit, but I'd be at the **edge** when it lands.
I'd be 23 with **debt** and maybe one job behind me.
do: Finish the degree and look for a **hardware** placement.
Learn one **AI tool** slowly in second year with a friend.
Go through the shop's **accounts** with my dad.
feel: **Nervous** but steadier than with two years.
S3.quote: With two years I'd be hanging on, but with five I can learn slowly, which is the only way I learn
fieldNote: Time lets her learn **slowly**, which suits her, and that moves her down from alarmed.
She wants a **friend** nearby when learning a new tool.
Her family **shop** is part of her plan, not separate from it.

steps.text: Look for a placement with a company that makes hardware
Learn one AI tool with Hana in second year
Put the shop's accounts into a spreadsheet with dad

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the fifth and last picture. It's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a long time and people should use it, though most won't. I'd tell my friends that we should keep learning and keep our options open. I'd say it quietly, but I'd mean it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel okay about me, because by 28 I'd have a career and savings, and I'd have learned the new tools at my own pace. I'd worry more about my parents, who'd be in their late fifties, and the shop. And my brother, who'd be finishing school just as it lands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree, get a stable first job, and start paying off the loan. I'd learn the new tools one at a time, and I'd help my parents decide whether to sell the shop or change it. I'd also save for my brother's education, because I'd like him to have more choice than I had.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopeful in a cautious way. I'd be glad to have time, but I'd be afraid of wasting it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do about your brother?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Start a small account for him now, even if it's only a little. I'd start a small savings account for my little brother, because I want him to have the choices I never had. He's good at maths, and he doesn't know it yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you stop yourself wasting the ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd write a plan for each year and show it to someone, probably my mum, because I'd feel bad if I didn't follow it. That's how I've always kept going.

say: I'd say ten years is a **long time** and people should use it.
I'd tell friends to keep learning and keep their **options** open.
think: I'd feel okay about **me**, with a career and savings by 28.
I'd worry about my **parents**, the shop, and my brother finishing school.
do: Finish the degree, get a **stable job** and start on the loan.
Learn new tools **one at a time**.
Help my parents decide about the **shop** and save for my brother.
feel: **Hopeful** in a cautious way, afraid of wasting the time.
S4.quote: I'd start a small savings account for my little brother, because I want him to have the choices I never had
fieldNote: Ten years eases her own **fear**, but the shop and her brother keep her uneasy.
She uses her **mum** as her accountability partner.
She wants her brother to have more **choice** than she did.

steps.text: Pay off the student loan steadily after the first job
Start a small savings account for my brother
Learn each new tool at my own pace, one a year

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because two years is too short for someone like me who learns slowly. What would help is a clear plan from the university about what they'll teach, and something to protect people with loans if the jobs change.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Just that quiet people aren't always calm. I look calm because I'm doing the sums in my head, and the sums keep telling me to be careful. I'd like someone to explain things to us plainly.

headlineQuote: I look calm because I'm doing the sums in my head, and the sums keep telling me to be careful
portrait: Aisha is an **18-year-old** computer engineering first-year living above her parents' corner shop with her little brother.
She is centrist, practical and resistant to change, and has never used an AI tool.
Her loan and the shop's falling takings are her **money** worries, and they stay in every scenario.
She learns slowly, prefers a friend nearby, and plans by doing sums and asking her mum.
Her mood runs from anxious to alarmed at two years, easing to uneasy with ten.
biggestWorry: The **2028** scenario worries her most, because two years is too short for her to learn.
whatWouldHelp: She wants a clear **plan** from the university and protection for people with loans.
